paper.title: Untying the Knot: How Child Support and Alimony Affect Couples' Dynamic Decisions and Welfare
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability: 'The data underlying this article were provided by Statistics Denmark and the Danish National Archives by permission. …

variables_mentioned: amount of maintenance payments made or received
which parent divorced couples' children live with

registers.role: linkage and controls: identifies the biological children a couple have together, distinguishing them from other children living in the household
variables_mentioned: number of (biological) children a couple have together

registers.name_in_paper: maintenance payer's tax declaration (recorded by tax authorities)
registers.role: treatment / outcome component: amount of maintenance payments

registers.name_in_paper: Danish Time Use Survey (DTUS) (SFI - Det Nationale Forskningscenter for Velfaerd 2001)
registers.role: moments for home production hours and the cross-sectional male-to-female consumption ratio; initial relative bargaining power

linkages: Spouses linked into couples through marital histories in the Danish register data, which cover all Danish individuals ever married during 1980-2013.
Biological children linked to the couple via the Danish birth register, so that children a couple have together are distinguished from other children in the household.
Divorced individuals linked to the amount of maintenance payments they make or receive (from the payer's tax declaration) and to the parent with whom the children live after divorce.

Register data combined with the 2001 Danish Time Use Survey at group level: married couples cannot be distinguished from cohabiting couples and divorced individuals cannot be distinguished from singles in the DTUS, so these groups are pooled.

sample.universe: All Danish individuals who have been married at some point during 1980-2013
selection_rules: Both spouses in their first marriage
At least one spouse working in at least one sampled year
Exclude couples where one spouse has a child from a previous relationship
Event studies only: balanced panel of divorcing spouses observed continuously for at least 2 years before and 6 years after divorce (42,290 divorcing couples)
Asset regressions only: exclude couples with assets above the 98th or below the second percentile

construction_notes: Hours worked are employer-recorded in five bins of weekly hours (<10, 10-19, 20-29, 30-37, and >=38); work hours are set to 0 for nonparticipation, 38 for full time and to the bin midpoint otherwise (see Lund and Vejlin 2015).
Household assets record net wealth: bank deposits, other financial assets and real assets net of loans and mortgage debt; positive when savings exceed debt and negative otherwise.
Median assets among divorcing couples are 22,475 DKK; the second percentile is -855,690 DKK.
Event-study coefficient estimates from specification (1) are normalised by adding the average of the outcome at divorce, E-hat[y_it | d_it = 1].

Household consumption expenditures are imputed from accounting identities on labour income, maintenance payments and changes in asset holdings; individual consumption is backed out using equivalence scales, a cross-sectional male-to-female consumption ratio from the DTUS and a linear approximation of the Danish tax system (Supplementary Material, Appendix B).
Divorcees who remarry or cohabit with a new partner are assumed to share finances with the new partner, whose labour income and assets enter the consumption imputation.
In the structural model one time period corresponds to 3 years; T = 10 working periods and T_R = 4 retirement periods; one year consists of 49 working weeks.
Weekly work hours in the model are restricted to {0, 10, 25, 34, 38}; the weekly time budget is fixed at H = 50 hours.
The status quo child support and alimony schedule is approximated by non-linear least squares at b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.
79% of women take custody of all children after divorce; the share taking custody of some children is 92%.

claims.statement: Around divorce, women reduce their weekly work hours by 0.76 hours over the first 6 years after divorce.

treatment.label: Divorce (event time relative to the year of divorce)

register_source.value: Danish administrative register data (Statistics Denmark 2024): individual marital history recorded from 1980; the paper names no register code or variable name

definition.value: d_it, a dummy variable that indicates whether individual i divorces in calendar year t; event-time dummies d_it-k for k = -2,...,+6 enter specification (1), so the treatment is measured in years relative to the calendar year of divorce.

timing.value: Calendar year of divorce, with event time from 2 years before to 6 years after divorce

outcome.label: Weekly work hours

register_source.value: Danish administrative register data (Statistics Denmark 2024); the paper names no register code or variable name

definition.value: Weekly work hours. Hours worked are employer-recorded in five bins of weekly hours (<10, 10-19, 20-29, 30-37, and >=38); the paper sets work hours to 0 in the case of nonparticipation, 38 in the case of full time and, if work hours fall into one of the bins, to the midpoint of the respective bin.

timing.value: Annually, event years -2 to +6 relative to the year of divorce

units.value: weekly work hours (change over the first 6 years after divorce)

magnitude.interpretation: The paper describes this as a tendency of women to 'reduce their work hours over the first 6 years after divorce'.

estimand.target_population: Danish individuals in first marriages who divorce and are observed in a balanced panel for at least 2 years before and 6 years after the divorce, 1980-2013
estimand.time_horizon: over the first 6 years after divorce

population.description: Divorcing Danish couples drawn from register data 1980-2013: both spouses in their first marriage, both aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, no child from a previous relationship; balanced panel of 42,290 divorcing couples observed at least 2 years before and 6 years after divorce.
population.selection: Conditioned on divorcing and on being observed continuously in the register panel for at least 2 years before and 6 years after the divorce; the underlying couple sample is conditioned on first marriage, ages 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year and no child from a previous relationship.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the timing of divorce across Danish couples observed in administrative registers 1980-2013, with age and calendar-year fixed effects absorbing age and time trends (specification (1), following Kleven et al. 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on age fixed effects and calendar-year fixed effects, variation in the timing of divorce separates changes that are associated with divorce from age and time trends; i.e. the event-time coefficients recover the counterfactual-mean change in the outcome at divorce.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that the event studies 'exploit variation in the timing of divorce to separate changes that are associated with divorce from age and time trends' and plots event years k = -2 and -1 in Figure 3; no formal pre-trend, placebo or balance test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on panel survival: only divorcing couples observed continuously for at least 2 years before and 6 years after divorce enter the balanced panel.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction; 42,290 divorcing couples satisfy the criteria.

key_assumptions.assumption: Event-time dummies are included for every k from -2 to +6 with no normalised reference period; identification of the plotted levels comes from adding Ê[y_it | d_it = 1] back to β̂_k.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Specification (1) and the normalisation described below it.

estimator.value: OLS event-study regression of specification (1) with age and calendar-year fixed effects, run separately for women and for men; plotted coefficients are β̂_k + Ê[y_it | d_it = 1]

estimation.specification: Equation (1): y_it = ω_t + υ_a(i,t) + Σ_{k=-2}^{6} β_k d_it-k + ν_it

evidence.annotation: Notes: The figures display the evolution of work hours (A), wages (B), assets (C), and household income net of maintenance (D) around divorce. Displayed are normalised coefficient estimates from event-study specification (1). The event-study regressions are run separately for women and men, include age and calendar year fixed effects and are based on a balanced panel of 42,290 divorcing couples who are observed for at least 2 years prior to and 6 years after divorce

evidence.how: Figure 3 plots 95% confidence bands but the paper prints no standard error, numerical confidence interval or p-value for any event-time coefficient; the tables carry no event-study coefficients either.
The paper prints no numerical pre-divorce mean of this outcome: the event-study figures are normalised by adding Ê[y_it | d_it = 1] and the pre-divorce level can only be read off the figure axis.
No standard deviation of the outcome is printed in the article.
The paper reports no formal pre-trend test, placebo test or balance table for the event studies.
The paper does not state how standard errors are clustered in the event-study regressions.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the targeted moments and reports asymptotic standard errors, but gives no formal identification argument or sensitivity analysis in the article.

key_assumptions.assumption: Preset parameters taken from the literature and external sources are correct: annual discount factor 0.98, risk aversion (eta) -1.5, annual interest rate 0.02, economies of scale (rho) 1.4023, retirement income 0.77 x w_sT h_s, tax rate 0.46, T = 10 periods of 3 years and T_R = 4 retirement periods.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 lists each preset parameter and its source.

key_assumptions.assumption: Fertility and custody are exogenous: a new child arrives with exogenous probability p(t, n_t), the probability that the mother is the custodial parent is fixed at 0.86, and the non-compliance and discontinuation probabilities for maintenance payments (0.17 and 0.12) are estimated directly and held fixed when policy is changed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 and the model section; the paper notes that 'Keeping fertility exogenous is in line with the previous literature'.

robustness_checks: Model fit to targeted moments (Figure 5 and Supplementary Material, Table G.2) and to untargeted relative consumption around divorce (Figure 6).

claims.statement: Raising the lump-sum component of child support, b0 so that child support is tripled leaves divorced women's mean weekly work hours (h_f) at 26.2 weekly hours, -3.5% relative to the status quo.

treatment.label: Child support policy parameter b0 raised to the value that would ceteris paribus triple child support payments

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: Policy parameter values b_k'' that would ceteris paribus TRIPLE child support payments relative to the approximated Danish status quo. Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

timing.value: Post-divorce maintenance regime imposed from the start of the simulation

outcome.label: Divorced women's mean weekly work hours (h_f)

register_source.value: Not a register variable: simulated from the structural model, which is estimated on Danish administrative register data (Statistics Denmark 2024) and the 2001 Danish Time Use Survey

definition.value: Mean weekly work hours in the simulated economy; in the model weekly work hours are chosen from the discrete set {0, 10, 25, 34, 38} and one model period corresponds to 3 years.

timing.value: Mean over divorced spouses in the simulated economy

units.value: weekly hours (simulated mean under the counterfactual policy; the status quo mean is the baseline)

magnitude.interpretation: -3.5% relative to the status quo, as printed in brackets in the table.

estimand.target_population: The 20,000 simulated couples drawn from the estimated model, which is calibrated to Danish couples in first marriages where both spouses are aged 25-58 and at least one spouse works in at least one sampled year
estimand.time_horizon: Mean over the simulated life cycle under the counterfactual policy regime

population.description: Simulated population of 20,000 simulated couples from the structural model estimated on Danish register data 1980-2013 merged with the 2001 Danish Time Use Survey; the estimation sample is couples in first marriages, both spouses aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, no child from a previous relationship (322,732 couples, 645,464 individuals, 4,312,826 couple-year observations).
population.selection: Couples where both spouses are in their first marriage and aged 25-58, at least one spouse is working in at least one sampled year, and neither spouse has a child from a previous relationship.

identification.source_of_variation: Counterfactual re-simulation of the estimated dynamic structural model under alternative maintenance-policy parameters, holding the estimated structural parameters fixed; N = 20,000 simulated couples.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dynamic structural model of married and divorced couples' labour supply, home production, savings and divorce -- CES home production, CRRA-type additively separable utility, random-walk love shocks, learning-by-doing human capital, limited commitment in marriage and non-cooperative play between ex-spouses -- is correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model fit to the 89 targeted moments (Figure 5) and to untargeted relative consumption around divorce (Figure 6); the paper states the model 'matches the considered empirical moments very well'.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 89 targeted empirical moments (conditional average weekly work hours, home production hours and wages by marital status and number of children; the fraction of ever-divorced couples by time since marriage; and the event-study coefficients for work hours and wages around divorce) identify the structural parameter vector theta.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the targeted moments and reports asymptotic standard errors, but gives no formal identification argument or sensitivity analysis in the article.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on first marriage, both spouses aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, and no child from a previous relationship.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction in Section 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Preset parameters taken from the literature and external sources are correct: annual discount factor 0.98, risk aversion (eta) -1.5, annual interest rate 0.02, economies of scale (rho) 1.4023, retirement income 0.77 x w_sT h_s, tax rate 0.46, T = 10 periods of 3 years and T_R = 4 retirement periods.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 lists each preset parameter and its source.

key_assumptions.assumption: Fertility and custody are exogenous: a new child arrives with exogenous probability p(t, n_t), the probability that the mother is the custodial parent is fixed at 0.86, and the non-compliance and discontinuation probabilities for maintenance payments (0.17 and 0.12) are estimated directly and held fixed when policy is changed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 and the model section; the paper notes that 'Keeping fertility exogenous is in line with the previous literature'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Policy invariance: the estimated preference, home-production, love-shock and wage-process parameters are invariant to the counterfactual child support and alimony policies, so the model can be re-simulated under the new policy with theta held fixed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: External validity checks comparing simulated responses to reduced-form estimates from Rossin-Slater and Wust (2018), Graham and Beller (1989), Cancian et al. (2013), Barardehi et al. (2020), Friday (2021), Ong (2024), Lafortune and Low (2023) and Rangel (2006) (Tables 11 and 12).

robustness_checks: External validity checks against reduced-form estimates from previous studies (Tables 11 and 12) and against evidence on unilateral divorce (Stevenson 2008), divorce legalisation (Bargain et al. 2012) and Danish taxable-income elasticities (Kleven and Schultz 2014).

estimator.value: Simulation of the structural model at the MSM parameter estimates under a counterfactual maintenance policy; reported values are simulated means over 20,000 couples

estimation.specification: Policy space (b0, b1, b2, bn, tau) approximating the Danish status quo at b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0, tau = 0.2

evidence.how: The article gives no formal identification argument, sensitivity analysis or specification test for the structural parameters beyond the model-fit figures.
No standard deviation of this outcome is printed in the article.
The simulated counterfactual outcomes are reported as point values only: the article prints no standard error, confidence interval or p-value for any policy simulation.

value.claimed_domain: Other OECD countries whose child support and alimony rules resemble the Danish system; the author argues the welfare maximising magnitude of child support can be viewed as a conservative lower bound when applied to other countries, and that the external validity checks support that the results extend to other time periods and countries including the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Switzerland.
boundary_conditions: Denmark has relatively low gender inequality in labour supply and earnings, so divorcing Danish women may be more economically self-sufficient and less in need of post-divorce consumption insurance.
Maintenance payments are relatively strictly enforced in Denmark and determined by rigid rules; enforcement is lower in many other countries.
Denmark's divorce rate since the 1990s has been higher than Germany's and the U.K.'s but markedly lower than the U.S. rate.

claims.statement: Raising the lump-sum component of child support, b0 leaves married women's mean weekly work hours (h_f) at 24.1 weekly hours, -19.9% relative to the status quo.

treatment.label: Child support policy parameter b0 raised to the value that would ceteris paribus lead to a ten-fold increase in child support payments

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: Policy parameter values b_k'' that would ceteris paribus lead to a TEN-FOLD increase in child support payments relative to the approximated Danish status quo. Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

claims.statement: Raising the lump-sum component of child support, b0 leaves married women's mean weekly home production hours (q_f) at 24.3 weekly hours, +32.1% relative to the status quo.

treatment.label: Child support policy parameter b0 raised to the value that would ceteris paribus lead to a ten-fold increase in child support payments

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: Policy parameter values b_k'' that would ceteris paribus lead to a TEN-FOLD increase in child support payments relative to the approximated Danish status quo. Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: Policy parameter values b_k'' that would ceteris paribus TRIPLE child support payments relative to the approximated Danish status quo. Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

identification.source_of_variation: Counterfactual re-simulation of the estimated dynamic structural model under alternative maintenance-policy parameters, holding the estimated structural parameters fixed; N = 20,000 simulated couples.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dynamic structural model of married and divorced couples' labour supply, home production, savings and divorce -- CES home production, CRRA-type additively separable utility, random-walk love shocks, learning-by-doing human capital, limited commitment in marriage and non-cooperative play between ex-spouses -- is correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model fit to the 89 targeted moments (Figure 5) and to untargeted relative consumption around divorce (Figure 6); the paper states the model 'matches the considered empirical moments very well'.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 89 targeted empirical moments (conditional average weekly work hours, home production hours and wages by marital status and number of children; the fraction of ever-divorced couples by time since marriage; and the event-study coefficients for work hours and wages around divorce) identify the structural parameter vector theta.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the targeted moments and reports asymptotic standard errors, but gives no formal identification argument or sensitivity analysis in the article.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on first marriage, both spouses aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, and no child from a previous relationship.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction in Section 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Preset parameters taken from the literature and external sources are correct: annual discount factor 0.98, risk aversion (eta) -1.5, annual interest rate 0.02, economies of scale (rho) 1.4023, retirement income 0.77 x w_sT h_s, tax rate 0.46, T = 10 periods of 3 years and T_R = 4 retirement periods.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 lists each preset parameter and its source.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 and the model section; the paper notes that 'Keeping fertility exogenous is in line with the previous literature'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Policy invariance: the estimated preference, home-production, love-shock and wage-process parameters are invariant to the counterfactual child support and alimony policies, so the model can be re-simulated under the new policy with theta held fixed.

boundary_conditions: Denmark has relatively low gender inequality in labour supply and earnings, so divorcing Danish women may be more economically self-sufficient and less in need of post-divorce consumption insurance.

claims.statement: The simulated average taxable income elasticity of divorced men with respect to the child support parameter b1 is 0.13.

treatment.label: Child support slope in the payer's income, b1, varied around the status quo

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: Policy parameter b1 of the child support schedule, which enters divorced men's budget constraint like a linear tax rate. Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

timing.value: Maintenance regime imposed for the whole simulated horizon

outcome.label: Average taxable income elasticity of divorced men with respect to b1

definition.value: Mean elasticity of male divorcees' labour income with respect to the child support policy parameter b1, computed from model simulations.

population.description: Simulated population of 20,000 simulated couples from the structural model estimated on Danish register data 1980-2013 merged with the 2001 Danish Time Use Survey; the estimation sample is couples in first marriages, both spouses aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, no child from a previous relationship (322,732 couples, 645,464 individuals, 4,312,826 couple-year observations).
population.selection: Couples where both spouses are in their first marriage and aged 25-58, at least one spouse is working in at least one sampled year, and neither spouse has a child from a previous relationship.

identification.source_of_variation: Counterfactual re-simulation of the estimated dynamic structural model under alternative maintenance-policy parameters, holding the estimated structural parameters fixed; N = 20,000 simulated couples.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dynamic structural model of married and divorced couples' labour supply, home production, savings and divorce -- CES home production, CRRA-type additively separable utility, random-walk love shocks, learning-by-doing human capital, limited commitment in marriage and non-cooperative play between ex-spouses -- is correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model fit to the 89 targeted moments (Figure 5) and to untargeted relative consumption around divorce (Figure 6); the paper states the model 'matches the considered empirical moments very well'.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 89 targeted empirical moments (conditional average weekly work hours, home production hours and wages by marital status and number of children; the fraction of ever-divorced couples by time since marriage; and the event-study coefficients for work hours and wages around divorce) identify the structural parameter vector theta.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the targeted moments and reports asymptotic standard errors, but gives no formal identification argument or sensitivity analysis in the article.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on first marriage, both spouses aged 25-58, at least one spouse working in at least one sampled year, and no child from a previous relationship.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction in Section 3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Preset parameters taken from the literature and external sources are correct: annual discount factor 0.98, risk aversion (eta) -1.5, annual interest rate 0.02, economies of scale (rho) 1.4023, retirement income 0.77 x w_sT h_s, tax rate 0.46, T = 10 periods of 3 years and T_R = 4 retirement periods.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 lists each preset parameter and its source.

key_assumptions.assumption: Fertility and custody are exogenous: a new child arrives with exogenous probability p(t, n_t), the probability that the mother is the custodial parent is fixed at 0.86, and the non-compliance and discontinuation probabilities for maintenance payments (0.17 and 0.12) are estimated directly and held fixed when policy is changed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 and the model section; the paper notes that 'Keeping fertility exogenous is in line with the previous literature'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Policy invariance: the estimated preference, home-production, love-shock and wage-process parameters are invariant to the counterfactual child support and alimony policies, so the model can be re-simulated under the new policy with theta held fixed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: External validity checks comparing simulated responses to reduced-form estimates from Rossin-Slater and Wust (2018), Graham and Beller (1989), Cancian et al. (2013), Barardehi et al. (2020), Friday (2021), Ong (2024), Lafortune and Low (2023) and Rangel (2006) (Tables 11 and 12).

robustness_checks: External validity checks against reduced-form estimates from previous studies (Tables 11 and 12) and against evidence on unilateral divorce (Stevenson 2008), divorce legalisation (Bargain et al. 2012) and Danish taxable-income elasticities (Kleven and Schultz 2014).

estimator.value: Simulation of the structural model at the MSM parameter estimates under a counterfactual maintenance policy; reported values are simulated means over 20,000 couples

estimation.specification: Policy space (b0, b1, b2, bn, tau) approximating the Danish status quo at b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0, tau = 0.2

evidence.how: The article gives no formal identification argument, sensitivity analysis or specification test for the structural parameters beyond the model-fit figures.
No standard deviation of this outcome is printed in the article.
The simulated counterfactual outcomes are reported as point values only: the article prints no standard error, confidence interval or p-value for any policy simulation.
The article prints no status-quo / baseline value of this outcome to compare against.

value.claimed_domain: Other OECD countries whose child support and alimony rules resemble the Danish system; the author argues the welfare maximising magnitude of child support can be viewed as a conservative lower bound when applied to other countries, and that the external validity checks support that the results extend to other time periods and countries including the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Switzerland.
boundary_conditions: Denmark has relatively low gender inequality in labour supply and earnings, so divorcing Danish women may be more economically self-sufficient and less in need of post-divorce consumption insurance.
Maintenance payments are relatively strictly enforced in Denmark and determined by rigid rules; enforcement is lower in many other countries.
Denmark's divorce rate since the 1990s has been higher than Germany's and the U.K.'s but markedly lower than the U.S. rate.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: my simulation results are small in magnitude and well within the 95% confidence intervals reported by Rossin-Slater and Wust's (2018) estimates

claims.statement: A simulated child support increase of 6% of divorced men's mean labour income lowers their log labour income by 0.02.

treatment.label: Increase in child support payments of 6% of divorced men's mean labour income

register_source.value: Not a register variable: a parameter of the maintenance-policy space that approximates the Danish statutory child support and alimony rules observed in the register data

definition.value: A simulated increase in child support payments of 0.06 x E[w_m^div h_m^div], matching the policy variation studied by Ong (2024). Child support is parameterised as cs_ft = n_ft^bn [b0 + b1 w_mt h_mt + b2 (w_mt h_mt - w_ft h_ft)] when the mother is custodial. b0 controls the lump-sum component of child support that is independent of the divorcees' labour incomes, b1 governs the responsiveness to the non-custodial parent's income, b2 the dependence on the income gap between non-custodial and custodial parent, and bn the curvature in the number of children. The approximated Danish status quo is b0 = 24,060, b1 = 0.028, bn = 0.79, b2 = 0 and tau = 0.2.

timing.value: Maintenance regime imposed for the whole simulated horizon

outcome.label: Change in log labour income of divorced men, Delta ln(w_m^div h_m^div)
